questions.title: DNS
questions.text: State what DNS stands for and describe its purpose.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Domain Name System (1)
- translates / resolves domain names into IP addresses (1)
scheme.model_answer: Domain Name System — it converts domain names such as nis.edu.kz into the IP addresses computers use.

questions.title: Name and IP
questions.text: Describe the relationship between an IP address and a domain name, and explain why domain names are used.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The IP address is the numerical identifier of the server the domain name represents (1)
- domain names are easier for people to remember / type than numbers (1)
scheme.model_answer: A domain name is a text label for the server's IP address; people use names because they are much easier to remember than numbers.

scheme.mark_scheme: gov (1)

questions.title: DNS servers
questions.text: Match each DNS server to its role.

right.text: Searches on behalf of the user's computer, usually run by the ISP

Stores the actual IP address records for one domain

questions.title: Order of a lookup
questions.text:
The steps of a DNS lookup are in the wrong order:

- **A** The resolver asks the root server
- **B** The browser checks its cache
- **C** The browser connects to the web server using the IP address
- **D** The authoritative server returns the IP address

Write the letters in the correct order.

scheme.mark_scheme: B, A, D, C (1 each)

questions.title: Caching
questions.text: Explain why DNS answers are cached by browsers and resolvers.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The IP address can be found without asking other DNS servers again (1)
- faster page loading / less DNS traffic / less load on servers (1)
scheme.model_answer: The stored IP address can be used next time without repeating the whole lookup, so websites open faster and there is less traffic to DNS servers.

questions.title: Distributed system
questions.text: Explain why DNS is distributed across many servers rather than stored on one central server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): too many names / requests for one server; no single point of failure / more reliable; faster — servers close to users; each organisation manages its own records
scheme.model_answer: One server could not hold billions of names or answer every request, and if it failed the whole Internet would stop working by name; many servers share the load and keep it reliable.

questions.title: DNS records
questions.text: Match each DNS record type to what it stores.

right.text: The IPv4 address of a name
The mail server for the domain
An alias pointing to another name

scheme.mark_scheme: A–IPv4, MX–mail, CNAME–alias.

questions.title: DNS spoofing
questions.text: Explain how DNS cache poisoning can be used to steal users' passwords.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- An attacker puts a false IP address for a real domain into a DNS cache (1)
- users typing the correct name are sent to a fake website that collects their login details (pharming) (1)
scheme.model_answer: The attacker changes the cached IP address for, say, a bank's domain to the address of a fake copy of the site; users type the right name but land on the fake page and enter their passwords.

parts.title: Explain
parts.text: Explain how the domain name is used to access a website. Include the role of Domain Name System (DNS) servers in your explanation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Up to 5 (1 each): user types URL / domain into browser; browser checks its cache / hosts file; request sent to DNS server / resolver which holds a list of domain names and IP addresses; if not found, request passed to other DNS servers (root → TLD → authoritative); IP address returned to the browser and cached; browser uses the IP address to contact the web server and request the page; error if name not found
scheme.model_answer: The user types the domain name in the browser, which first checks its cache. If the IP address is not there, it asks the DNS resolver, which looks it up and, if needed, asks a root server, then the .kz TLD server, then the domain's authoritative server. The IP address is returned and cached, and the browser uses it to connect to the web server and request the page.

scheme.mark_scheme: No need to repeat the full lookup (1); faster access / less network traffic / less load on DNS servers (1)
scheme.model_answer: The IP address is already stored, so the lookup does not have to be repeated and the site opens faster.

parts.title: Protocol
parts.text: Explain why the URL begins with https rather than http.

scheme.model_answer: HTTPS encrypts the data sent between the browser and the school's server, so it cannot be read or altered if intercepted.

questions.title: DNS servers
questions.text: DNS is a distributed, hierarchical system of servers.

parts.title: Server roles
parts.text: Describe the role of each server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Root: refers to the correct TLD server (1). TLD: knows the servers responsible for domains in that TLD (1). Authoritative: holds the records / IP address for the domain and returns it (1)
scheme.model_answer: Root: points the resolver to the server for the top-level domain. TLD server: points to the servers holding a particular domain. Authoritative server: stores the domain's IP address and gives it to the resolver.

parts.title: Distributed
parts.text: Explain **two** advantages of DNS being distributed across many servers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): shares the load of billions of requests; no single point of failure; faster responses from nearby servers; each organisation updates its own records
scheme.model_answer: The huge number of requests is shared between many servers, and if one server fails others still answer.

parts.title: Risk
parts.text: Explain how an attacker could misuse DNS to direct users to a fake website, and **one** way to protect against this.

scheme.mark_scheme: False IP address inserted into DNS cache / server (1); users typing the real name reach the fake site and may enter personal data (1); protection: DNSSEC / check HTTPS certificate / trusted DNS resolver (1)
scheme.model_answer: By DNS cache poisoning, the attacker stores a fake IP address for a real domain, so users are sent to a copy of the site and give away passwords. DNSSEC signs DNS records so false ones can be detected.

summary: Why the Internet needs the Domain Name System, how IP addresses and domain names are related, how domain names are organised into levels and zones, which DNS servers exist and who manages them, how a name is resolved step by step with caching, the main DNS records and risks, and the structure and parts of a URL.

blocks.content: Every device that sends or receives data on the Internet — a web server, a laptop, a phone, a smart TV — is identified by an **IP address**. An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written as four decimal numbers separated by dots, for example `185.22.66.10`; an IPv6 address is a 128-bit number written in hexadecimal, for example `2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334`. Routers use these numbers to decide where each packet goes, in the same way that a postal service uses a postcode and a house number. Computers are very good at working with numbers like this, but people are not. Nobody wants to remember that the school website is at `185.22.66.10`, the online diary is at `91.201.214.5` and a video site is at `142.250.74.46`.

To solve this problem, the Internet gives servers **names** as well as numbers. We type `nis.edu.kz` or `google.com` into the browser, and somewhere in the background the name is changed into the IP address that the computer actually needs. The system that does this translation for the whole Internet is the **Domain Name System (DNS)**.

A **unique numerical address** given to every device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol. It **identifies the device** and lets data be **routed** to it (IPv4: 32 bits, e.g. 185.22.66.10; IPv6: 128 bits).
An **easy-to-remember text name** that identifies a server (or a group of servers) on the Internet and **stands for its IP address**, e.g. `nis.edu.kz`, `egov.kz`, `google.com`.

A **distributed, hierarchical** system of **servers** (a database spread across many computers) that **translates domain names into IP addresses**, so that people can use names while computers use numbers. The translation is called **name resolution**.

The main purpose of DNS is **name resolution**: when a program is given a domain name, DNS finds the matching IP address. This one job brings several important benefits, and an exam answer that "describes the purpose of DNS" should mention more than just "it changes names into numbers".

items: **Names are easier to remember than numbers.** People can remember `kaspi.kz` after seeing it once. A meaningful name also tells the user something about the site — the organisation, the country, the type of service.

**Names stay the same when numbers change.** A company may move its website to a new hosting provider, or a school may replace its server. The new server has a new IP address, but the organisation simply **updates the DNS record**. Users keep typing the same name, bookmarks still work and links in old e-mails still work. Without DNS, every move would mean telling every user a new number.

**One name can lead to many servers.** Large services such as YouTube or a national e-government portal cannot run on one computer. DNS can return **different IP addresses** for the same name, sending users to the nearest or least busy server (this is called **load balancing**).

**One server can host many names.** A small hosting company may run hundreds of websites on one physical server with one IP address. Each site has its own domain name; the web server looks at the name in the request to decide which site to show.

**DNS finds other services, not only websites.** The same system tells an e-mail server where to deliver mail for `@nis.edu.kz` (an MX record), and tells other computers which servers are responsible for a domain.

blocks.caption: DNS translates a name that people remember into a number that routers use

blocks.text: The relationship between an IP address and a domain name

blocks.content: The domain name and the IP address are two ways of identifying the **same server**. The IP address is the **real, numerical identifier** that is used for routing; the domain name is a **label for people** that DNS links to that number. It is helpful to compare this with a phone's contact list: you tap "Mum", but the phone actually dials a number. The contact list is the "DNS" of your phone.
The relationship is **not always one-to-one**:

items: **One name → several IP addresses.** `google.com` has many addresses around the world; DNS may give a user in Almaty a different address from a user in London.
**Several names → one IP address.** A hosting server at one IP address may hold `school1.kz`, `bakery-astana.kz` and `myblog.kz`.
**One name → IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.** The same name can have a 32-bit (IPv4) and a 128-bit (IPv6) address at the same time.
**The link can change.** The owner can point the name at a new IP address at any time by changing the DNS record.

blocks.title: IP address vs domain name
rows: Levels separated by dots, read right to left
Changes if the server or provider changes
Usually stays the same for years
No — a site can be reached by IP alone

blocks.title: Opening the school website by name and by number
blocks.content: A student types `nis.edu.kz` into Chrome. DNS returns the address `185.22.66.10` (example value) and the page opens. The student then types `http://185.22.66.10` directly. On a simple server the same page may open, which shows that the **name was only a label for the number**. On a server that hosts many sites, typing the bare IP may show an error or a default page, because the web server uses the **name** in the request to choose which of its sites to send. This is why we say one IP address can serve several domain names.

"Describe the relationship between an IP address and a domain name [1]" — a good one-line answer: **the domain name is a text name that DNS converts into the IP address (the numerical identifier) of the server**.

In the early days of the Internet (the 1970s), every computer kept a single text file called **HOSTS** that listed every name and its address. A central office updated the file and everyone downloaded a new copy. This worked for a few hundred computers but broke down as the network grew: the file became huge, it was always out of date, and every new name had to go through one office. DNS was designed in 1983 to replace it, and its key idea is that the database is **distributed** — split into pieces that are stored on **millions of servers** around the world.
Distribution brings clear advantages:

items: **Scale.** There are hundreds of millions of registered domain names and billions of look-ups every day. No single computer could store all the records or answer all the requests.
**No single point of failure.** If one DNS server breaks, others hold copies of the same data (every domain must have at least two name servers) and the system keeps working.
**Speed.** Resolvers are placed close to users (in the ISP or the school network), and answers are cached, so most look-ups are answered in a few milliseconds.
**Local control.** Each organisation manages the records for **its own** domain. NIS updates the records of `nis.edu.kz` without asking anyone else; Kaspi updates `kaspi.kz`.

blocks.title: Central HOSTS file vs distributed DNS
rows: One file copied to every computer
Wait for the central office and a new copy of the file
Owner changes its own server; change spreads within hours
File grows with every name on the Internet
Each server holds only its own part
If the central office fails, no updates
Many copies; no single point of failure

blocks.title: The hosts file still exists
blocks.content: Your computer still has a small `hosts` file (on Windows in `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`). It is checked **before** DNS. A school technician can use it to block a site by pointing its name to `127.0.0.1` — and malware sometimes edits it to redirect users to fake sites.

The second part of the objective is the **organisation** of DNS. Domain names are not just random words: every name has a fixed **structure**, and that structure matches the way the servers are organised. Understanding the structure lets you answer questions such as "state the top-level domain of …" or "state the second-level domain of …", which appear often in Paper 1.

A domain name is made of **labels** separated by **dots**. Each label is one **level** of the hierarchy. The name is read **from right to left**: the label on the far right is the most **general** level, and each label to its left is more **specific**. At the very top, to the right of the last label, there is an invisible **root**, written as a single dot. The full name `www.nis.edu.kz.` really ends with that dot, although we never type it.
The **last (right-most) part** of a domain name, directly below the root, e.g. `.kz`, `.com`, `.org`. It shows the **country** or the **type of organisation**.

The part of the name **directly to the left of the TLD**, e.g. `edu` in `nis.edu.kz` or `google` in `google.com`. It is usually the name of the **organisation** or, in some countries, a **category** (edu, gov, com).

Any domain that is **part of a larger domain** and is written to its left, e.g. `sk.nis.edu.kz` is a subdomain of `nis.edu.kz`. The owner of a domain can create subdomains **without registering** them again.

blocks.title: The levels of www.sk.nis.edu.kz
rows: The top of the whole hierarchy
The web server inside that domain

blocks.content: Notice that in `google.com` the second-level domain is `google` (the organisation), while in `nis.edu.kz` it is `edu` (a category) and the organisation is at the third level. Both are correct: the level number always comes from **counting labels from the right**, not from what the label means. Many country-code domains, such as `.kz`, `.uk` and `.jp`, have category second-level domains (`edu.kz`, `gov.kz`, `co.uk`, `ac.jp`), while others are used directly (`kaspi.kz`, `egov.kz`).

blocks.content: Top-level domains are divided into groups. The two groups that every student must know are **generic** TLDs and **country-code** TLDs.

items: **Generic TLDs (gTLDs)** describe the **type of organisation**: `.com` (commercial), `.org` (non-profit organisations), `.net` (network providers), `.edu` (US universities), `.gov` (US government), `.info` (information). Since 2013 hundreds of **new gTLDs** have been added, such as `.app`, `.shop`, `.online`, `.bank`.

**Country-code TLDs (ccTLDs)** have **two letters** and belong to a **country or territory**: `.kz` (Kazakhstan), `.ru` (Russia), `.uk` (United Kingdom), `.de` (Germany), `.cn` (China). Each country decides its own rules — for example, some `.kz` names require the server to be located in Kazakhstan.
**Internationalised domain names (IDN)** allow letters that are not Latin. Kazakhstan has the Cyrillic ccTLD `.қаз`, so a name can be written fully in Kazakh.

blocks.title: Generic vs country-code top-level domains
rows: A registry company chosen by ICANN
Set by the country (may require local presence)

blocks.content: Because names must be **unique** — there can only be one `nis.edu.kz` in the world — someone must keep order. Management is also hierarchical:

items: **ICANN** (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) coordinates the whole system: it manages the **root zone** and decides which TLDs exist.
Each TLD has a **registry** that keeps the list of all names in that TLD and runs its servers. The `.kz` and `.қаз` registry is run by **KazNIC** (the Kazakhstan Network Information Centre).

Organisations and people buy names through **registrars** — companies accredited to sell names (for example, a hosting provider). The owner pays to **register** the name for a period, usually one year, and must renew it, otherwise it becomes free for someone else.
The owner then decides which **name servers** hold the records for the domain, and can create any subdomains inside it.

blocks.title: Registering a domain for a bakery in Astana
blocks.content: Aigerim opens a bakery called "Nan House" and wants the site `nanhouse.kz`. (1) She checks with a registrar that the name is **free** — it must be unique in the `.kz` zone. (2) She pays the registrar for one year; the registrar sends her details to the **KazNIC registry**, which adds `nanhouse.kz` to the `.kz` zone. (3) She chooses a hosting company; its name servers `ns1.host.kz` and `ns2.host.kz` are written into the registry, so the `.kz` servers now know **where to send questions** about her domain. (4) On those name servers the hosting company creates an **A record** `nanhouse.kz → 89.218.10.20` (example) and a subdomain `shop.nanhouse.kz` for the online shop — no new registration is needed for a subdomain. (5) Next year she must **renew** the name, or it will be released.

"State the **second-level** domain of www.sk.nis.edu.kz" → **edu**. Always count from the **right**: kz = top (1st) level, edu = 2nd, nis = 3rd, sk = 4th; `www` is the host. "State the **TLD**" → **kz**.

The tree of names would be useless without computers that store it and answer questions about it. These computers are **DNS servers** (also called **name servers**). Their organisation **mirrors** the tree of names: there are servers for the root, servers for each top-level domain and servers for each organisation's domain.

The tree of names is cut into pieces called **zones**. A zone is the part of the tree that one organisation manages. The root zone is managed for ICANN; the `kz` zone is managed by KazNIC; the `nis.edu.kz` zone is managed by NIS. A server that holds the **original, official records** for a zone is called **authoritative** for that zone. When the owner of a zone wants another organisation to manage a part of its tree, it **delegates** that part: the `kz` zone does not store the address of `www.nis.edu.kz`; it only stores a pointer saying "for anything ending in `nis.edu.kz`, ask these name servers". This idea — each level only knows **where to find the next level** — is what makes DNS scale to the whole Internet.
A DNS server that holds the **official records** for a domain (zone) and gives the **final answer** about it, e.g. the server that stores the IP address of `www.nis.edu.kz`.

A DNS server, usually run by the **ISP** or the **school network**, that receives a request from a user's computer and **does all the searching** — asking other DNS servers — until it can return the IP address.

blocks.text: The four types of DNS server

items.title: Resolver (recursive server)
items.content:
- The **first** DNS server the computer talks to; its address is set automatically by the router (DHCP) or by hand (e.g. 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1).
- Does the work **for** the user and **caches** answers so the next user gets them instantly.

items.title: Root name servers
items.content:
- At the **top** of the hierarchy. They do not know any website addresses; they know the servers of **every TLD**.
- There are 13 named root server identities (a.root-servers.net … m.root-servers.net), copied to more than a thousand machines worldwide.

items.title: TLD name servers
items.content:
- One set for each top-level domain, e.g. the `.kz` servers run by KazNIC.
- They know which **authoritative servers** hold each domain in their TLD.

items.title: Authoritative name servers
items.content:
- Hold the actual **records** (A, MX, CNAME …) for a domain.
- Run by the organisation itself or by its hosting company; at least **two** for reliability.

blocks.text: How the hierarchy of servers divides the work

blocks.content: The beauty of this design is that **no server needs to know everything**. A root server knows only about 1 500 TLDs. A `.kz` server knows the name servers of every `.kz` domain, but not the addresses of the computers inside them. The NIS name server knows every computer in `nis.edu.kz`, but nothing about `kaspi.kz`. When a question arrives, each server either **answers** it (if it is authoritative) or gives a **referral** — "I don't know, but ask that server, which is one level closer to the answer". A resolver follows the referrals down the tree until it reaches the authoritative server. This process is studied step by step in the next lesson.

blocks.title: The four types of DNS server
rows: A referral to the TLD server
Below the root (one set per TLD)
Name servers of every domain in the TLD
A referral to the authoritative server
The real records: A, AAAA, MX, CNAME…
The final answer: the IP address

blocks.title: Who knows what about www.nis.edu.kz?
blocks.content:
- The **root server** is asked "where is www.nis.edu.kz?" It does not know, but it sees the name ends in `.kz` and answers: "ask the `.kz` servers, here are their addresses".
- The **`.kz` TLD server** does not know either, but its zone contains a delegation for `nis.edu.kz` and it answers: "ask `ns1.nis.edu.kz`".
- The **authoritative server `ns1.nis.edu.kz`** holds the record `www → 185.22.66.10` and gives the final answer.
- Three servers, three short answers — and none of them had to store the whole Internet.

- Saying DNS is **one big server** or "a website". DNS is a **distributed** system of many servers organised in a hierarchy.
- Saying DNS **stores web pages**. It stores **names and the matching IP addresses** (and other records); pages are stored on **web servers**.
- Counting domain levels from the **left**. Levels are counted from the **right**: the TLD is the right-most label.
- Thinking `www` is a domain level that every site must have. `www` is just a **host name**; many sites work without it.
- Confusing the **registrar** (sells the name) with the **registry** (keeps the list for the whole TLD) and with **ICANN** (coordinates everything).

theory.title: Exam practice: domain names and DNS

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe the purpose of the Domain Name System. [2]**
DNS **translates / resolves domain names into IP addresses** (1) so that users can use **easy-to-remember names** instead of numerical addresses / the IP address can change without users noticing (1).

**Q: Describe the relationship between an IP address and a domain name. [1]**
The domain name is a text label that DNS links to the **IP address (numerical identifier)** of the server (1).

**Q: State the second-level domain and the top-level domain of www.ast.nis.edu.kz. [2]**
Second-level: **edu** (1). Top-level: **kz** (1).

**Q: Explain why DNS is a distributed system rather than one central database. [3]**
There are **too many names / requests** for one server to store or answer (1); if one server fails the others still work — **no single point of failure** (1); each organisation can **manage its own records** / servers close to users make look-ups **faster** (1).

**Q: Describe the role of a root server and of an authoritative server. [2]**
A root server knows the addresses of the **TLD servers** and refers the request to the correct one (1). An authoritative server holds the **actual records** for a domain and returns the **final IP address** (1).

**Q: Give one difference between a gTLD and a ccTLD, with an example of each. [2]**
A gTLD shows the **type of organisation**, e.g. `.org` (1); a ccTLD has two letters and shows the **country**, e.g. `.kz` (1).

- Answering "the purpose of DNS" with only "it is a system of names" — always say it **converts names into IP addresses**.
- Writing `.edu` as the TLD of `nis.edu.kz` — the TLD is the **last** label, `kz`.
- Describing a root server as "the server that has all addresses" — it only knows the **TLD servers**.

theory.title: How a domain name is resolved

blocks.content: In the first lesson we saw **what** DNS is and how names and servers are **organised**. Now we follow a single request from the moment a student presses Enter in the browser to the moment the page starts to load. This process is called **name resolution** or a **DNS lookup**, and "explain how a domain name is used to access a website" is one of the most common long questions on this topic.
The process of **finding the IP address** that matches a domain name by **querying DNS servers** (and caches), so that the computer can connect to the correct server.

Suppose a student in Shymkent types `https://www.nis.edu.kz/en/news.html` into the browser for the first time today. Before any web page can be requested, the computer needs the IP address of `www.nis.edu.kz`.

blocks.title: The full DNS lookup
items: **Browser cache.** The browser checks whether it has recently looked up `www.nis.edu.kz`. If the IP address is in its cache and has not expired, it uses it at once and skips every step below.
**Operating system.** The browser asks the operating system. The OS checks the **hosts file** and its own **DNS cache** (shared by all programs on the computer).

**Query to the resolver.** If the address is still not found, the computer sends a **DNS query** to the **resolver** configured on the network — usually the ISP's or the school's DNS server. The query asks: "What is the A record of www.nis.edu.kz?"
**Resolver cache.** The resolver checks its own cache. Because it serves thousands of users, a popular name is often already there and the answer is returned immediately.
**Root server.** If not cached, the resolver asks a **root server**. The root server replies with a **referral**: the addresses of the `.kz` TLD servers.
**TLD server.** The resolver asks a `.kz` server. It replies with a referral to the **authoritative servers** for `nis.edu.kz` (e.g. `ns1.nis.edu.kz`).

**Authoritative server.** The resolver asks `ns1.nis.edu.kz`, which looks in its zone and returns the **A record**: `www.nis.edu.kz → 185.22.66.10`, together with a **TTL** (how long the answer may be cached).
**Answer returned and cached.** The resolver **stores** the answer in its cache and sends it back to the computer, which also caches it.
**Connection to the web server.** The browser now opens a connection to **185.22.66.10** (port 443 for HTTPS) and sends an HTTP request for `/en/news.html`. DNS's job is finished.

**If the name does not exist**, the authoritative or TLD server replies "no such domain" (NXDOMAIN) and the browser shows an error such as "This site can't be reached — server IP address could not be found".

blocks.content: There are two styles of DNS query in the process above, and they explain why the resolver is called a "recursive" server.

items: The query from the **computer to the resolver** is **recursive**: the computer says "give me the final answer, do whatever you need to do". The computer then simply waits.

The queries from the **resolver to the root, TLD and authoritative servers** are **iterative**: each of those servers gives the best answer it has — often only a referral — and the resolver must ask the next server itself.

blocks.content: This division of work keeps the root and TLD servers simple and fast: they never have to search on anyone's behalf; they just answer from their own zone. The hard work and the memory (cache) sit in the resolvers, which are close to the users.

blocks.title: Recursive vs iterative DNS query
rows: "Tell me the answer **or** who to ask next"
The server that receives it (the resolver)
The server that sent it (the resolver)
Light work for the root and TLD servers

blocks.content: If every look-up went all the way to the root servers, the root servers would receive billions of requests an hour and every page would load slowly. DNS avoids this with **caching**: every answer is **stored** for a while by the resolver, the operating system and the browser. The owner of the domain decides **how long** an answer may be stored by setting the **TTL (time to live)** in the record, in seconds. A TTL of 3600 means "you may keep this answer for one hour".

A temporary store of **recent DNS answers** (names and IP addresses) kept by the browser, the operating system and the resolver, so that repeated look-ups can be answered **without asking other DNS servers**.
The number of **seconds** a DNS answer may be **kept in a cache** before it must be looked up again; it is set by the owner of the domain in each record.

Caching has clear benefits: **repeat visits are much faster** (a cached answer takes under a millisecond instead of tens of milliseconds), **less traffic** crosses the Internet, and the root and TLD servers are protected from overload. It also has a cost: when the owner **changes** a record, users may still be sent to the **old IP address** until the cached copies expire. This is why technicians lower the TTL a day before moving a website to a new server.

blocks.title: Why the second visit is faster — and why a changed site may not appear at once
blocks.content: At 09:00 the first student in a class opens `bilimland.kz`. The school's resolver has nothing cached, so it queries the root, the `.kz` server and the authoritative server: the look-up takes about 80 ms. The answer has a **TTL of 3600 s**, so the resolver keeps it until 10:00. At 09:01 twenty-five more students open the same site: the resolver answers each of them from its **cache** in about 1 ms, and no requests leave the school. At 09:30 the site owner moves the website to a new server and changes the A record. Students in the school still reach the **old** address until **10:00**, when the cached answer expires and the resolver looks the name up again. Clearing the browser and OS cache (for example `ipconfig /flushdns` on Windows) does not help if the **resolver** still has the old answer.

An authoritative server does not only store "name → IP address". Its zone contains several kinds of **resource records**, each holding a different type of information about the domain. The most important are listed below; you are expected to know A and MX, and the others help you understand how e-mail and aliases work.

blocks.title: Common DNS records
rows: An alias — another name to look up
The authoritative servers of the domain

blocks.title: How e-mail uses DNS
blocks.content: A parent sends an e-mail to `teacher@nis.edu.kz` from Gmail. Gmail's server does not need a web page; it needs to know **which server accepts mail** for `nis.edu.kz`. It asks DNS for the **MX record** of `nis.edu.kz` and receives `mail.nis.edu.kz`. It then asks for the **A record** of `mail.nis.edu.kz` and receives its IP address, for example `185.22.66.25`. Only then does it connect and deliver the message. If the MX record were missing or wrong, the e-mail would bounce even though the website `www.nis.edu.kz` worked perfectly — a clear sign that DNS is about **services and addresses**, not about web pages.

blocks.text: Risks to DNS and how they are reduced

blocks.content: Because almost every Internet action begins with a DNS look-up, DNS is an attractive target for attackers. If DNS fails, websites that are working perfectly **cannot be reached by name**; if DNS lies, users are sent to the **wrong server** without noticing.

items: **DNS spoofing / cache poisoning.** An attacker tricks a resolver into storing a **false IP address** for a real name, for example `kaspi.kz → attacker's server`. Every user of that resolver is then sent to a **fake website** that looks like the real one and steals their passwords. This attack is called **pharming**. Because the answer is cached, the damage lasts for the whole TTL.
**Hosts-file attacks.** Malware edits the computer's hosts file, which is checked before DNS, to redirect names on that one computer.
**DDoS on DNS servers.** Flooding a DNS provider with requests can make thousands of websites unreachable at the same time, as happened in a large attack on a DNS provider in 2016.
**Hijacking the domain.** If an attacker steals the owner's registrar password, they can change the NS records and take control of the whole domain.

blocks.title: DNS threats and protection
rows: Resolver stores a false IP; users go to a fake site
One PC is redirected by malware
Names cannot be resolved; sites unreachable
Many servers in many places; anycast; filtering
Strong password and 2FA at the registrar; registry lock
User enters data on a copy of the site
**HTTPS** certificate check — browser warns if the certificate does not match

blocks.content:
- Leaving out **caching** in a "describe the steps" answer — the browser, OS and resolver caches are checked **first**.
- Saying that the **root server** returns the IP address — it only refers the resolver to the **TLD** server; the **authoritative** server gives the final answer.
- Thinking the browser downloads the page **from the DNS server** — DNS only returns the address; the page comes from the **web server**.
- Mixing up **phishing** (a fake link in a message) with **pharming** (a correct name redirected by poisoned DNS).
- Writing that TTL is the time a **packet** lives — in DNS, TTL is how long an **answer** can stay in a cache.

A domain name tells the browser **which server** to contact. But a server holds thousands of resources — pages, pictures, PDF files, videos — and the browser also needs to know **how** to talk to the server. All this is given by a **URL**.

The full **address of a resource** (web page, file, image, video) on the Internet. It states the **protocol** to use, the **server** (domain name or IP address) to contact and the **location of the resource** on that server.

blocks.caption: Parts of a URL

blocks.content: The first part, ending with `://`, tells the browser **which set of rules** to use to fetch the resource. `http` is the Hypertext Transfer Protocol; `https` is HTTP **secured with encryption** (TLS), shown by a padlock; `ftp` is the File Transfer Protocol; `mailto:` opens an e-mail program. The protocol matters because the same server may offer different services, and because only `https` protects passwords and personal data on the way.

After `://` comes the **domain name** of the server, such as `www.nis.edu.kz`. This is the part that is passed to **DNS** to find the IP address — so this is where the two objectives of the topic meet. An IP address can be written here instead (`http://192.168.1.1` for a home router), and `localhost` means the user's own computer.

A colon and a number after the domain name choose the **service** on the server. Port **80** is the default for HTTP and **443** for HTTPS, so they are normally **left out**. A port is written only when a non-standard one is used, e.g. `http://localhost:3000` for a website being developed on your own laptop.

After the domain comes the **path**: the folders on the server, separated by forward slashes `/`, and usually the **file name** of the resource with its extension, such as `/en/students/timetable.html`. The path works like the folders on your own disk. Modern sites often hide file names (`/news/2026/` instead of `/news/2026/index.php`), but the path still identifies the resource.

A question mark `?` starts **parameters** sent to the server, written as `name=value` pairs joined with `&`, for example `?class=11A&day=mon`. A search engine uses it to send the search words (`?q=binary+tree`), and an HTML form with the GET method puts its fields here. The server reads these values and builds the page.

A hash `#` followed by a name points to a **position inside the page**, such as a heading. The fragment is **not sent to the server**; the browser uses it to scroll to the right place after the page has loaded.

blocks.title: Parts of a URL
rows: **How** to transfer the resource (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP)
**Which server**; converted to an IP address by **DNS**
Service on the server (80 = HTTP, 443 = HTTPS)
Parameters sent to the server (`name=value`, joined with `&`)
A position inside the page (not sent to the server)

blocks.text: How the browser uses each part

blocks.content: When the user presses Enter, the browser takes the URL apart from left to right. It reads the **protocol** and decides to use HTTPS. It reads the **domain name** and asks DNS for its IP address (the look-up from the previous section). It reads the **port** — or uses 443 because none is written — and opens a connection to that IP address and port. It then sends a request that contains the **path, file name and query**, for example `GET /en/students/timetable.html?class=11A`. The server finds the file, runs any program that needs the query values, and sends back the page. Finally the browser looks at the **fragment** and scrolls to the "monday" heading. In this way one line of text contains everything the browser needs: **how**, **where**, **what** and **which part**.

blocks.title: Taking apart three real-style URLs
blocks.content:
- `http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/George.jpg` — protocol **http**; host name **commons.wikimedia.org** (TLD `org`, second level `wikimedia`, subdomain `commons`); file location **/wiki/George.jpg** (folder `wiki`, file `George.jpg`).
- `ftp://files.school.kz/homework/task1.pdf` — protocol **ftp** (file transfer, not a web page); host **files.school.kz**; path `/homework/`; file `task1.pdf`.
- `https://shop.kz:8080/catalog/phones.php?brand=samsung&sort=price#reviews` — protocol **https**; host **shop.kz**; port **8080** (non-standard, so it must be written); path `/catalog/`; file `phones.php` (a server-side script); query with **two** parameters `brand=samsung` and `sort=price`; fragment `reviews`.

blocks.title: URL vs domain name vs IP address
rows: One **resource** on that server, with the protocol

blocks.content:
- Calling the whole URL "the domain name". The domain name is **only one part** of the URL.
- Using back slashes `\` in a path — URLs use **forward slashes** `/`.
- Saying the fragment `#…` is sent to the server — it is used only by the **browser**.
- Thinking `https` is a different website from `http` — it is the **same** server reached with a **secure protocol**.
- Forgetting that a port is written only when it is **not the default**.

theory.title: Exam practice: DNS look-up and URLs

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain how the domain name is used to access a website, including the role of DNS servers. [5]**
The user types the URL / domain name into the browser (1). The browser / OS checks its **cache** for the IP address (1). If not found, a request is sent to the **DNS server (resolver)**, which looks up the domain name in its records / cache to find the **IP address** (1). If that server does not know it, the request is passed to **other DNS servers** up the hierarchy — root, TLD, authoritative (1). The **IP address is returned** to the browser (and cached), which uses it to **connect to the web server** and request the page (1).

**Q: State what is meant by the TTL of a DNS record. [1]**
The time (in seconds) for which the answer may be **kept in a cache** before it must be looked up again (1).

**Q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of DNS caching. [2]**
Advantage: repeated look-ups are **faster** / less DNS traffic, because the answer is taken from the cache (1). Disadvantage: after a record changes, users may be sent to the **old IP address** until the cached answer expires (1).

**Q: Give one example of a URL indicating protocol, host name and file location. [1]**
`https://www.nis.edu.kz/en/timetable.html` (1).

**Q: For the URL `https://edu.gov.kz/ru/docs/plan.pdf?year=2026`, identify the protocol, the domain name, the path, the file name and the query. [3]**
Protocol **https**, domain **edu.gov.kz** (1); path **/ru/docs/**, file name **plan.pdf** (1); query **year=2026** (1).

**Q: Describe how DNS cache poisoning can lead to pharming. [2]**
An attacker puts a **false IP address** for a real domain name into a DNS cache (1), so users who type the correct name are sent to a **fake website** that collects their data (1).

- Writing only "DNS finds the website" in a 5-mark answer — give each **step**: cache, resolver, other servers, IP returned, connection to the web server.
- Writing `www.nis.edu.kz/en` as the domain name — the path is **not** part of the domain name.
- Calling the query string "the file" — the file name ends before `?`.
